summary: This document defines an RTCP Extended Report block that reports a post-repair loss count metric for RTP applications. It also introduces a repaired loss count metric in the same block.

eli5.summary: When some video packets get lost and then fixed, this lets a receiver report how many were still missing after fixing.

questions: how to report repaired packet loss in rtp
how to measure rtp loss repair effectiveness
subtitle: A compact RTCP report that tells a sender how many lost packets were fixed and how many stayed lost.

tldr.problem: Standard RTCP reports count packets lost before any repair, so a sender cannot tell how well retransmission or forward error correction is working. The existing per-packet report from RFC 5725 costs more bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7509 defines an RTCP XR block, block type 33, that carries a post-repair loss count and a repaired loss count over an explicit range of sequence numbers.
tldr.outcome: The sender or a third party can work out how many packets are still lost, how many were repaired and so how effective the repair methods are.

today: RFC 7509 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2015. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Pre-Repair Counts Are Not Enough
sections.content:
RTCP Sender and Receiver Reports (RFC 3550) include the cumulative number of packets lost. This document calls that the pre-repair loss metric, because it is measured on the media stream before any loss-repair mechanism, such as retransmission (RFC 4588) or Forward Error Correction (RFC 5109), is applied.

Recovering a packet does not lower the fraction lost or the cumulative loss in those reports. So the sender cannot judge how well its repair mechanism performs from them alone. RFC 5725 addressed this with a run-length encoded block, but its packet-by-packet reporting has a higher overhead than other report blocks.
sections.eli5: Normal reports only say how many packets went missing, even if some were later replaced. It is like a score sheet that never erases a mistake after you fix it.

sections.title: The Two New Metrics
sections.content:
The new block reports a post-repair loss count: the number of packets still lost after one or more repair mechanisms have been applied. It also reports a repaired loss count, which is the number of packets fully repaired. With the pre-repair count, the repaired count lets a sender or third-party entity calculate the pre-repair loss over the same range.

Both metrics count only primary source RTP packets, meaning the original packets the sender sent for the first time. They work at packet level, not slice or picture level, so partly recovering a packet does not count as repairing it. The metrics are measured at the RTP receiver and apply to any RTP application, especially one that uses loss repair.
sections.eli5: One number says how many lost things stayed lost. The other says how many were found again. Only the first copy of each thing counts, and half-fixed does not count as fixed.

sections.title: The Report Block Format
sections.content:
The block is identified by block type (BT) 33. Its fields are:

  • Reserved (8 bits): MUST be set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers.
  • Block length (16 bits): MUST be 4. A block with any other value MUST be discarded.
  • SSRC of source (32 bits): as defined in RFC 3611.
  • begin_seq (16 bits): the first sequence number the block reports on.
  • end_seq (16 bits): the last sequence number reported on, plus one.
  • Post-repair loss count (16 bits): packets finally lost in that range. It MUST NOT count lost packets that could still be repaired.
  • Repaired loss count (16 bits): packets fully repaired in that range.
sections.eli5: The report is a small form. It names the stream, gives the first and last packet numbers it covers, and fills in two boxes: still lost and fixed.

sections.title: Cumulative and Interval Reports
sections.content:
Because some packets missing in one RTCP interval may be repaired later, the block states its sequence number range explicitly. Only packets that have no further chance of being repaired, and packets that have been repaired, are included.

In a cumulative report, begin_seq is set to the first packet of the session and stays fixed. Combined with the cumulative loss from an RTCP Receiver Report, the sender can compute: still-to-be-repaired lost packets = cumulative number of packets lost - cumulative post-repair loss count - cumulative repaired loss count.

In an interval report, begin_seq and end_seq follow the highest sequence numbers of consecutive Receiver Reports. This is NOT RECOMMENDED: in the RFC's example, packets 17 and 19 are lost in interval A and repaired in interval B, but interval B starts at 20, so they are never reported. Implementations that want those reported MUST NOT align the range to RTCP intervals. They may instead choose a range that covers several intervals and overlaps earlier reports.
sections.eli5: If you only count what happened this week, a toy lost on Friday and found on Monday gets missed. So the report should look at a longer stretch of packets, not just one short window.

sections.title: Signaling with SDP
sections.content: RFC 3611 lets endpoints announce XR blocks in SDP with the rtcp-xr attribute, although XR blocks MAY also be used without prior signaling. This document adds a new xr-format value, post-repair-loss-count, to that attribute. In an offer/answer exchange, the rules for unilateral rtcp-xr parameters in RFC 3611 apply.
sections.eli5: Before a call, each side can say 'I can send this kind of report' using a short agreed word.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The block adds no new security considerations beyond RFC 3611, and because it carries no per-packet statistics, the confidentiality risk noted there does not apply. An attacker could still put incorrect numbers in these reports, which would affect the performance of loss-repair mechanisms. Where security matters, implementations should apply encryption and authentication, following the guidance in RFC 7202, for example with the AVPF profile together with Secure RTP (SAVPF, RFC 5124).

IANA assigned block type value 33 in the RTCP XR Block Type Registry and registered the SDP parameter post-repair-loss-count.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person could write false numbers on the form, so important reports should be locked and signed.
